newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dell to detail Europe results, online sales.
newsitem.headline: Dell to detail Europe results, online sales.

text.p: Dell Computer Corp, following up a robust first-quarter earnings announcement, planned to detail gains in European markets on Thursday as well as a rapid expansion into selling computers over the Internet.
Dell on Tuesday said first-quarter European sales rose 38 percent to $644 million, helping lift worldwide sales 58 percent to $2.59 billion and net income 141 percent rpt 141 percent to $198 million.

The company on Thursday would expand on results in Germany and France, where sales increased more than 50 percent, and outline an online strategy that was generating more than $1 million in sales each month in Germany, said Hans-Juergen Mamitzsch, managing director of Dell Computer GmbH in Langen.
"This is the most effective way of selling product," Mammitzsch told Reuters. "It is a competitive advantage."
Mammitzsch declined to elaborate on first-quarter European results ahead of Thursday's series of press conferences.
But market researcher Dataquest said Dell's European market share rose to 5.9 percent in the first quarter, up from 4.5 percent in the same period in 1996.
Dell leaped ahead of Hewlett-Packard Co. and Siemens Nixdorf Informationsysteme AG to become Europe's third largest vendor after IBM Corp. and Compaq Computer Corp., Dataquest said.
Dell aimed to continue its market share gains by expanding electronic commerce to account for about 10 percent of German sales by the end of the year, Mammitzsch said.

Right now about $1.1 million in orders come in each month from Deutsche Telekom AG's T-Online, Germany's largest online service, and another 180,000 came from buyers who read Dell's home page on the Internet.
He expected sales from the Internet to rise rapidly as Dell upgrades the system. Dell online sales in the United States have already reached $1 million per day.

In Europe, the company wanted to allow buyers to check on orders and delivery dates via computer by early next year, and would add an online configurator -- a program that lets users choose from a wide variety of hard drives, memory configurations, software and other options.
Online buyers can now only select from a limited number of the most popular PCs configuration, Mammitzsch said.
Dell was also building online order sites on the Intranets -- or internal computer networks -- of large corporate customers.

"That really reduces the cost of sales," Mammitzsch said. "It frees our account executives to concentrate on the real job of taking care of the customer and not get tied up with administration and paperwork."

For each sales lead generated by these online systems, Dell has about five dollars in costs -- compared to $25 to $100 per-lead costs for traditional media like magazine advertisements, Mammitzsch said.
Dell had boosted online sales systems in Germany, France, Britain and the Benelux countries, and planned to expand into other parts of Europe this year, he said.
